THE ABSTRACT AND TITLE PAGE

1. THE FUNCTIONS OF THE ABSTRACT

- Present the aims of the study

- Provide the background and context of the study

- Describe methods used in the study

- Report the key findings of the study

- Report the contributions of the study to the field of knowledge

2. THE CONTENT AND STRUCTURE OF THE ABSTRACT

1. Move 1: Introduction

1.2 Research aims (research questions, hypotheses,...)

Article title: Corrective feedback: Beliefs and practices of Vietnamese primary EFL teachers

Source: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/1362168820931897

teachers
Source: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/1362168820931897

This study investigates Vietnamese EFL teachers’ beliefs and practices regarding oral corrective feedback, exploring and seeking to explain some of the relationships between beliefs and classroom practices. Data were collected in primary schools in Vietnam, and consist of 24 classroom observations and interviews with six teachers. Overall, the teachers showed high levels of awareness of the benefits of oral corrective feedback. They nominated pronunciation errors as the most important target for correction in the primary context

iation errors as the most important target for correction in the primary context. In practice, although pronunciation and grammar accounted for the majority of the total errors, leading to the majority of total feedback moves, the frequency of feedback per error was much higher for vocabulary errors. Prompts were reported by teachers to be more effective and more favourable than reformulations, but this preference was not reflected in the classroom observations, in which a large number of didactic recasts were used

he classroom observations, in which a large number of didactic recasts were used. The observed discrepancies are interpreted in relation to contextual factors and the influence of different sets of beliefs on practices. It was also noted that the linguistic realizations of these teachers’ feedback moves contained some inaccuracies. Implications for educational practice are discussed.

Practice 2: Emotion regulation and psychological well-being in teacher work engagement: A case of British and Iranian English language teachers

Source: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0346251X2030806X
Source: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0346251X2030806X

Employing a sequential explanatory mixed-methods approach, this study investigated the role of emotion regulation and psychological well-being (PWB) as predictors of work engagement through using 108 British and 255 Iranian English language teachers as a sample. A multi-group structural equation modelling was performed to identify differences and similarities in the way emotion regulation and PWB could predict work engagement among British and Iranian English teachers. The valid measuring instruments of the three constructs were administered to collect the data in the two contexts

f the three constructs were administered to collect the data in the two contexts. The results demonstrated measurement invariance, including both metric and scalar invariance, revealing that the constructs underlying the three scales possessed the same theoretical structure across two groups (i.e., British vs. Iranian). It was also revealed that both emotion regulation and PWB significantly predicted work engagement for the whole sample of British and Iranian teachers. However, PWB appeared to be a stronger predictor of work engagement

an teachers. However, PWB appeared to be a stronger predictor of work engagement. Moreover, some cross-cultural differences were identified in the regression coefficients. On the whole, the association of the PWB and work engagement was stronger for British teachers. The qualitative data analysis uncovered a number of categories and themes contributing to explaining differences between British and Iranian teachers. The results and implications are further discussed.

Introduction to Large Language Models (LLM)
Large language models are deep neural networks trained on vast text data.
They can generate human-like text, answer questions, and solve complex problems.
However, LLMs suffer from hallucination and lack private domain knowledge.
To overcome this limitation, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is introduced.

To overcome this limitation, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is introduced.

--- [Page 2] ---
Chapter 2: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
A typical RAG pipeline contains three major stages:
1. Indexing: Documents are chunked and transformed into vector embeddings.
2. Retrieval: When a user query arrives, relevant chunks are retrieved.
3. Generation: Chunks are provided to the LLM as ground truth context.

# AI Engineering Cheat Sheet

1. Data Preparation:
- Split raw documents with recursive or semantic chunking.
- Maintain overlap (e.g., 50-100 characters/tokens) to preserve boundary context.

2. Retrieval Optimization:
- Combine Dense Vector search (Jina, BAAI, OpenAI) with Sparse Lexical search (BM25).
- Normalise BM25 scores before reciprocal rank fusion or weighted sum.

3. Evaluation:
- Decompose generated responses into atomic claims.
- Evaluate Faithfulness and Groundedness using an LLM-as-a-judge.

Who Owns the Sidewalk? Informal Street Vending in Ho
 Chi Minh City through Sociological Theory
 Weekly Homework, Session 02 – Major Sociological Theory
1. Introduction
On the sidewalks and in the alleyways of Ho Chi Minh City (HCMC), informal street vending is
at once a livelihood, a public service and a target of municipal campaigns. Because it places
economic survival, urban governance and the use of public space in direct contact, it is a useful
case for testing sociological theory. This essay applies three perspectives from class: Structural

ociological theory. This essay applies three perspectives from class: Structural
Functionalism, Conflict Theory and Interactionism, with most weight on the first two. It argues
that they answer different questions: Functionalism explains why vending persists and why
some regulation is needed, Conflict Theory explains who bears the cost of that regulation, and
Interactionism explains why the same street can be read as “disorder” or as “city life”.
2. Four Types of Research Questions
Following the definitions used in class, a factual question asks how or why things occur; a

he definitions used in class, a factual question asks how or why things occur; a
comparative question asks how things differ and why; a developmental question asks what can
be improved and how it could be implemented; and a theoretical question asks which theories
explain the factors involved and whether there is a gap between theory and reality. For street
vending they can be posed as follows.
 Factual. How does street vending currently operate in HCMC, and why do many
rural-to-urban migrants, who often lack a local household registration (hộ khẩu), turn to it

an migrants, who often lack a local household registration (hộ khẩu), turn to it
rather than to formal employment?
Comparative. How do enforcement and vendors’ income stability differ for mobile cart
vendors in District 1 compared with peripheral working-class districts such as Bình Tân or
District 12, and why? Keeping the vendor type constant makes location the main variable. A
comparison over time (for example, before and after the 2016–2017 clearance campaign, or
with the relative tolerance that followed Đổi Mới in 1986) would follow the same logic.

e relative tolerance that followed Đổi Mới in 1986) would follow the same logic.
Developmental. What could improve the situation for both vendors and other street users,
and how could it be implemented? For example, designated trading zones and hours
negotiated with vendors, combined with basic hygiene support.
Theoretical. Which theories best explain the pattern of tolerance and clearance, and is there
a gap between what the theories predict and what happens on the street? For instance, if
regulation simply restored urban balance, we would not expect enforcement to vary so much

n simply restored urban balance, we would not expect enforcement to vary so much
between districts.
3. Structural Functionalism: Vending as Part of a Working System
Functionalism, associated with Durkheim and Parsons, sees society as a structure of interrelated
parts, like organs serving the body as a whole. It distinguishes manifest functions, which are
visible and intended, from latent functions, which are invisible and unintended, and it considers
dysfunction, where a part stops serving its function and society restructures around alternatives

--- [Page 2] ---
(Merton, 1968).
The manifest function of vending is plain: it supplies cheap, decentralised meals and everyday
goods to factory workers, students and low-income households. A latent function concerns
migrants. Durkheim’s concept of anomie describes the strain felt when old norms no longer
apply and new ones have not yet been absorbed, as for a villager arriving in a fast-growing city.
Vending requires little capital and no formal hiring, so it absorbs people the formal labour
market does not, and this may ease that strain. It is latent because neither vendors nor the city

and this may ease that strain. It is latent because neither vendors nor the city
set out to create such a buffer; it is an unintended by-product of many individual survival
decisions. The same accessibility keeps living costs lower for workers, though this overlaps
with Marxist arguments about the cost of reproducing labour.
The dysfunction is that the sidewalk, planned as a space for pedestrian movement, no longer
fully serves that purpose where it is occupied by stalls; congestion and food-safety risks add to

purpose where it is occupied by stalls; congestion and food-safety risks add to
this. Zoning, licensing and scheduled hours can then be read as the “restructuring” that
Functionalism expects. In answer to the theoretical question, this perspective leans toward
“administrative necessity”.
Limitation. Functionalism tends to treat regulation as neutral. It cannot easily explain why
enforcement is uneven across space or why vendors seldom shape the rules.
4. Conflict Theory: Vending as a Struggle over Space

ors seldom shape the rules.
4. Conflict Theory: Vending as a Struggle over Space
Conflict Theory holds that social structures arise from struggle between groups with different
interests and resources, and that power and resources are unequally distributed. Applied to
cities, it draws on Lefebvre’s (1968) idea of the “right to the city”, developed by Harvey (2008)
as a collective right to shape urban life. Sidewalks are a scarce resource valued differently by
different groups: by vendors as a workplace, and by the state and investors as part of an image

s: by vendors as a workplace, and by the state and investors as part of an image
of a modern, attractive city that supports tourism and investment.
Read this way, clearance campaigns are not simply neutral traffic management. Kim (2015)
shows that in HCMC, sidewalks are a contested site where ideas of modernity are pursued
through the regulation of everyday street life. Vendors, who typically have limited political
voice and few alternatives, bear the costs. The comparative question becomes significant here:

alternatives, bear the costs. The comparative question becomes significant here:
if enforcement is consistently stricter in areas of high property value, that pattern would support
a class-based interpretation, and it would be an example of a gap between the Functionalist
prediction and reality. In answer to the theoretical question, this perspective leans toward
“spatial exclusion”.
Limitation. Conflict Theory can understate real problems, since congestion and food-safety
risks affect other residents too, including low-income ones. It also risks portraying the state as a

esidents too, including low-income ones. It also risks portraying the state as a
single actor, whereas local officials may negotiate or tolerate vending in practice (Turner &
Schoenberger, 2012).
5. Interactionism: How the Street Is Given Meaning
Interactionism, founded by Mead (1934), holds that meaning is built through everyday
interaction and that people act according to how they define situations. As class put it, planners

--- [Page 3] ---
assign functions to space, but users create meanings through use. The same alley can therefore
be defined by officials as an untidy obstruction and by customers and neighbours as a valued
place to eat and socialise. Labelling matters too: vendors described as “illegal” may accept,
resist or reinterpret that label, which is an empirical question of the kind labelling theory raises.
This lens adds what the other two omit, namely how vendors and users themselves experience
the space day to day, and it suggests that any developmental proposal should be tested against

to day, and it suggests that any developmental proposal should be tested against
those meanings.
6. Synthesis and Position
The three perspectives work as diagnostic lenses: Functionalism asks whether the arrangement
serves a real function; Conflict Theory asks whose interests it serves and who is excluded;
Interactionism asks how people actually interpret the space. Functionalism accounts for the
persistence of vending and the legitimacy of some regulation. On the evidence discussed here,
Conflict Theory offers the stronger explanation of how campaigns operate, because it explains

ry offers the stronger explanation of how campaigns operate, because it explains
variation in enforcement and the exclusion of vendors from decisions. Interactionism explains
why the conflict is also symbolic.
This points to a policy direction: regulation is more defensible when it includes vendors, for
example through zones and hours negotiated with them, than when it only removes them. Street
vending in HCMC therefore cannot be reduced to “disorder”. It reflects an ongoing tension
between the city’s ambition to be an orderly global metropolis and its dependence on an

the city’s ambition to be an orderly global metropolis and its dependence on an
informal economy. Answering the factual and comparative questions with real data would show
which theory the evidence supports most strongly.
